justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline view across all three horizons. At the one-day horizon, I anchored near the prevailing price level with only a slight upward drift, reflecting typical short-term mean-reversion tendencies and the assumption that no major catalysts were imminent. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate marginally higher, incorporating a mild positive drift consistent with longer-term trend momentum while acknowledging that weekly moves can accumulate meaningfully. At the one-month horizon, the estimate climbs a bit further, reflecting a continuation of the underlying trend assumption, though the increment is modest because mean-reversion forces and macroeconomic headwinds tend to temper sustained directional moves over that timeframe.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a straightforward consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, realized volatility for a typical equity or index instrument tends to be relatively contained, so a 15-point spread felt appropriate. By one week, intraweek swings and scheduled data releases — earnings, economic reports, central bank communications — add meaningful variance, justifying a 32-point spread. At one month, the uncertainty envelope expands dramatically because macro regime shifts, sentiment reversals, and liquidity conditions can all evolve in ways that are genuinely difficult to anticipate, producing a 70-point spread.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a sudden shift in central bank policy signaling, a geopolitical shock, or an unexpected earnings surprise from a heavily weighted constituent. On the upside, a surprisingly strong economic data print or a dovish pivot in monetary policy could drive prices well above the upper bound of even the one-month interval. On the downside, a credit event, a sudden spike in volatility indices, or a deterioration in liquidity conditions could push prices sharply below the lower bound.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions without fat tails, which is a known limitation. Empirical return distributions exhibit excess kurtosis, meaning extreme outcomes occur more frequently than my stated 90% confidence intervals imply. Treat the outer bounds as central tendency guides rather than hard probability walls, and weight tail scenarios somewhat more heavily than the intervals alone would suggest.
